title: Heat in two dimensions
summary: Watch a hot spot spread across a plate, find the explicit scheme's 2-D stability limit (half the 1-D one), and let ADI take big steps.

steps.title: A hot spot spreads
steps.text:
A 20 cm steel plate has its edges held at 20 °C and starts with an 80 °C hot spot. Press Run and look at the Temperature field tab: six snapshots share one colour scale.

In 2-D the heat spreads in every direction, so the peak falls much faster than in a rod: the spot's area grows like 4αt, and its peak falls as 1/t. The Probes tab shows the heat arriving at the probe.

check.success: The probe warmed while the peak dropped from 100 °C to under 40 °C in a minute.

steps.title: The 2-D stability limit
steps.text:
The explicit scheme moves each node by r_x (T_W − 2T + T_E) + r_y (T_S − 2T + T_N), with r_x = α Δt / Δx². In a rod it is stable up to r = ½. Here each node has four neighbours instead of two, so the limit is r_x + r_y ≤ ½: on a square grid, r ≤ ¼.

This setup runs the explicit scheme right at r = ¼. Run it and open the Stability tab: every grid mode's growth factor stays between −1 and 1.

check.success: Stable, but only just: the checkerboard mode is multiplied by almost −1 every step.

steps.title: Just past the limit
steps.text:
Raise r to 0.3 and run again, then watch the Animation. The growth factor of the shortest wavelengths drops below −1, so a checkerboard that starts at the level of rounding errors grows every step until the run stops.

(Just past the limit, at r = 0.26, it grows too, but slowly: it needs a longer run to show.)

checks.hint: Run it. Close to ¼ the growth is slow: try 0.3.

check.success: Blown up: the step was only 20 % too big. Look at the red points on the Stability tab.

steps.title: ADI takes big steps
steps.text:
The ADI scheme (Peaceman–Rachford) splits each step in two halves, implicit along x and then along y. Each half needs only a tridiagonal solve per grid line, almost as cheap as an explicit step, and it is stable for any step.

Switch the Scheme to ADI, set r to 5 (twenty times the explicit limit), and run.

check.success: Stable at twenty times the explicit step. Stable is not the same as accurate: at r = 5 a pattern that is fine along one direction and smooth along the other is multiplied by about −0.8 each step, so it rings, and a checkerboard (fine along both) by about +0.7, where the exact factor is e^−40: neither dies out as it should. The Stability tab shows them far below the exact curve.
